title: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ βάτος
part: The Fox and the Bramble (Chambry 31 · Perry 19)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 31 (= Perry 19). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ φραγμὸν ἀναβαίνουσα, ἐπειδὴ ὀλισθήσασα καταπίπτειν ἔμελλεν, ἐπελάβετο πρὸς βοήθειαν βάτου.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx phragmon anabainousa, epeidē olisthēsasa katapiptein emellen, epelabeto pros boētheian batou.
sentences.l: A fox climbing a fence, when, having slipped, she was about to fall down, took hold, for help, of a bramble.
sentences.i: A fox was climbing a fence, and when she slipped and was on the point of falling, she caught hold of a bramble to save herself.
sentences.n: ἐπιλαμβάνομαι takes the genitive of what one grasps (βάτου) — worth noticing, because the same verb comes back in the bramble's answer and carries the whole joke. A φραγμός is a fence or hedge, often the thorn hedge itself, which is why a bramble is there to be grabbed.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ τοὺς πόδας ἐπὶ ταῖς ἐκείνης κέντροις αἱμάξασα καὶ ἀλγήσασα πρὸς αὐτὴν εἶπεν· « Οἴμοι· καταφυγοῦσάν με γὰρ ἐπὶ σὲ ὡς ἐπὶ βοηθὸν σὺ χεῖρον διέθηκας.
sentences.tr: Kai dē tous podas epi tais ekeinēs kentrois haimaxasa kai algēsasa pros autēn eipen· « Oimoi· kataphygousan me gar epi se hōs epi boēthon sy cheiron diethēkas.
sentences.l: And so, having bloodied her feet on that one's prickles and being in pain, she said to her: « Alas! For you have put me, having fled for refuge to you as to a helper, in a worse state.
sentences.i: And when she had made her feet bloody on the bramble's thorns and was in pain, she said, « Oh! I ran to you for help, and you have left me worse off than I was.
sentences.n: διατίθημι with an adverb means to put someone into a state: χεῖρον διέθηκας, 'you have disposed me worse'. γάρ is postpositive and never stands first; here it follows the whole phrase καταφυγοῦσάν με, which counts as a single word-group. The speech opens here with « and is not closed until the end of the bramble's reply: Chambry follows French practice, marking the change of speaker with a dash inside a single pair of guillemets. One oddity of the text as printed: ταῖς is feminine while κέντροις is neuter — the article does not agree with its noun. It is left exactly as Chambry prints it.

sentences.t: — Ἀλλ’ ἐσφάλης, ὦ αὕτη, φησὶν ἡ βάτος, ἐμοῦ βουληθεῖσα ἐπιλαβέσθαι, ἥτις πάντων ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι εἴωθα. »
sentences.tr: — All’ esphalēs, ō hautē, phēsin hē batos, emou boulētheisa epilabesthai, hētis pantōn epilambanesthai eiōtha. »
sentences.l: — But you went wrong, you there, says the bramble, in having wished to take hold of me — I who am accustomed to take hold of everything. »
sentences.i: « But you made your mistake, my good woman, » said the bramble, « in wanting to lay hold of me, when it is I who lay hold of everything. »
sentences.n: The point is one verb used both ways: the fox 'takes hold of' the bramble, the bramble 'takes hold of' all comers — ἐπιλαβέσθαι against ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι. ἥτις … εἴωθα is a relative clause with a first-person verb, 'I, who am in the habit'; Greek allows the person of the antecedent to carry through. ὦ αὕτη is a brisk, familiar way of addressing a female — 'you there', 'my good woman'. φησίν is the historic present, dropped in mid-speech as the narrator's tag.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων μάταιοι ὅσοι βοηθοῖς προστρέχουσιν οἷς τὸ ἀδικεῖν μᾶλλον ἔμφυτον.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn mataioi hosoi boēthois prostrechousin hois to adikein mallon emphyton.
sentences.l: The fable shows that so too, of men, foolish are all those who run for help to helpers in whom doing-wrong is rather what is inborn.
sentences.i: The fable shows that so too men are foolish when they run for help to those whose nature it is rather to do wrong.
sentences.n: Two moral formulas welded together: ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι, 'the fable shows that', and then οὕτω καί, 'so too', which usually opens a moral on its own. τὸ ἀδικεῖν is an articular infinitive doing duty as a noun, 'the doing of wrong', subject of an understood ἐστί with ἔμφυτον. ὅσοι is 'as many as', hence 'all who'.
